implementation_notes: asyncio is the native realization: task-group members are the fan-out, leaving the group is the wait-for-all gather, asyncio.timeout(budget) supplies the deadline, and asyncio.as_completed(timeout=...) streams replies so a first-acceptable policy can answer early. The semantics that decide the merge policy are explicit in the docs: TaskGroup cancels the remaining tasks when one of them fails, while gather(return_exceptions=True) collects every outcome; and neither gather nor as_completed cancels the tasks that are still running when the timeout fires, so a partial gather has to reap them itself. concurrent.futures.wait(timeout=...) is the synchronous mirror of the same idea (see the second variant).
code_sketch:
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tasks = [tg.create_task(ask(r, client)) for r in recipients]
try:
    async with asyncio.timeout(budget):
        await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)   # partial gather: no cancellation
except TimeoutError:
    for t in tasks:                 # reap the stragglers explicitly
        t.cancel()
offers = [t.result() for t in tasks if t.done() and not t.cancelled() and t.exception() is None]
pitfalls: Plain gather propagates the first exception immediately while the other coroutines keep running as orphans; return_exceptions=True is what makes a partial gather possible.
as_completed(timeout=...) raises TimeoutError but leaves the remaining tasks running: cancel them, or the event loop keeps working for a request that already returned.
Blocking library calls inside coroutines serialise the loop - wrap them in asyncio.to_thread or move to a ThreadPoolExecutor.

variants.name: ThreadPoolExecutor with futures.wait/as_completed timeouts
variants.idiom_name: Executor.submit per recipient + concurrent.futures.wait(fs, timeout=...) / as_completed
variants.implementation_notes: In synchronous code the fan-out is executor.submit per recipient and the gather is wait(fs, timeout=budget, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED/FIRST_EXCEPTION) or as_completed(fs, timeout=...), which yields futures in completion order and therefore supports a first-answer policy; Executor.map is the shorthand when results may be consumed in recipient order. The timeout does not cancel anything, so the stragglers must be reaped with Future.cancel() or Executor.shutdown(cancel_futures=True), and ProcessPoolExecutor is the variant to reach for when the recipients are CPU-bound rather than remote.
variants.code_sketch:
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    futures = {pool.submit(ask, r): r for r in recipients}
    done, pending = concurrent.futures.wait(
        futures, timeout=budget, return_when=concurrent.futures.FIRST_COMPLETED)
    for f in pending:                     # the timeout reaps nothing by itself
        f.cancel()
offers = [f.result() for f in done if not f.cancelled() and f.exception() is None]
pitfalls: wait()/as_completed() timeouts return partial futures and cancel nothing: unfinished futures keep occupying pool threads until they are cancelled or the pool shuts down.
Executor.map raises the first exception while iterating and returns results in input order, which hides how late each reply arrived and makes per-recipient failure reporting awkward.
The GIL limits CPU-bound parallelism: threads help blocking I/O, while CPU-heavy recipients need ProcessPoolExecutor (and picklable callables).
